displayQuote: If you want to know what the Lord God thinks of money, just look at those to whom he gives it

meta.title: Who really said "If you want to know what the Lord God thinks of money, just look at those to whom he gives it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Quoted everywhere as Dorothy Parker. She said it in 1956 — and credited Maurice Baring. The thought is over four centuries old.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you want to know what the Lord God thinks of money, just look at those to whom he gives it'?
meta.ogDescription: Parker said it out loud and credited someone else. Quote Investigator traces the thought back to Luther’s Table Talk.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — a saying centuries older
answer.sourceLine: Parker did use the line — in her 1956 Paris Review interview — but she introduced it as Maurice Baring’s remark, and Baring’s own novel had credited it to Swift. Quote Investigator traces the thought back to Martin Luther’s Table Talk ↗, published in German in 1566 and in English in 1659.

docMeta.dd: Martin Luther, recorded by his students
Capt. Henrie Bell, second edition, 1659, p. 90

source.excerpt: Our Lord God commonly giveth Riches to such gross Asses, to whom hee affordeth nothing else that is good.
trail: Quote Investigator’s survey of the saying ↗ prints a chronology running from Luther (German 1566, English 1659) through Matthew Poole (1696), Richard Steele in The Tatler (1710), Jonathan Swift (1720), Alexander Pope (1727), Anne Marsh-Caldwell (1851), Thomas Guthrie (1861) and Austin O’Malley (1915).

The same page quotes Parker’s 1956 Paris Review interview directly: “I like to think of Maurice Baring’s remark: ‘If you would know what the Lord God thinks of money, you have only to look at those to whom he gives it.’” She is quoting, and says so in the same sentence.
Quote Investigator adds that Baring’s 1927 novel Tinker’s Leave has the character Troumestre credit the thought to Swift — so even Parker’s named source was passing it along.
Wikiquote files this exact popular wording under Dorothy Parker → Misattributed ↗, pointing to Thomas Guthrie and to Pope’s Thoughts on Various Subjects (1727).
source.excerptNote: The earliest form Quote Investigator documents ↗, quoted from Henrie Bell’s 1659 English translation of Luther’s Table Talk. The wording now pinned on Dorothy Parker is far smoother, and very much later.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status is asserted, because this exact modern wording matches no source we could document. It reads as a smoothed version of what Parker said in The Paris Review in 1956, which is in copyright; the older forms it descends from — Bell’s 1659 English Table Talk, Swift in 1720, Pope in 1727, Guthrie in 1861 — are long in the public domain.

author.name: Martin Luther
author.heading: About Martin Luther
author.metaLine: 1483–1546 · German priest, theologian and seminal figure of the Reformation
author.bio: Martin Luther (10 November 1483 – 18 February 1546) was a German priest, theologian, author and hymnwriter, and the seminal figure of the Protestant Reformation. Table Talk, the collection in which the earliest form of this saying appears, gathers remarks his students recorded at his dinner table; it was first published in German in 1566, after his death, and reached English in Henrie Bell’s translation of 1659.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is quoted as pure Dorothy Parker: the perfect acid remark about the rich, from the woman best equipped to make it. Parker did say it, in print — and in the same breath told her interviewer it belonged to somebody else.

items.why: In her 1956 Paris Review interview Parker introduces the line as “Maurice Baring’s remark”, not her own — Quote Investigator quotes the passage in full ↗.
Quote Investigator records ↗ that Baring’s 1927 novel Tinker’s Leave gives the thought to a character who credits it to Swift, rather than claiming it.
Quote Investigator documents ↗ a Swift letter of August 1720 with a related but different wording — the idea, not this sentence.
Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ begins with Luther’s Table Talk, published in German in 1566 and in English in 1659.

misattribution.truthLine: It is a commonplace Quote Investigator traces across 460 years ↗, and Parker never claimed it as hers.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Parker is a magnet for other people’s epigrams, and this one fits her so well that nobody checks. It has her cadence, her contempt, and her subject.

What makes the case unusual is that the correction is sitting inside the very interview people quote from. Parker names Maurice Baring in the same sentence. The attribution did not survive because the evidence was buried — it survived because the line was too good to interrupt.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the thought surfacing again and again in different clothes: Luther on the “gross Asses” God hands riches to (1566/1659), Matthew Poole on riches thrown away “upon the basest of men” (1696), Richard Steele in The Tatler (1710), Swift in a letter of 1720, Pope in Thoughts on Various Subjects (1727), Thomas Guthrie in 1861 and Austin O’Malley in 1915.
By the time it reached Parker in 1956 it had been in circulation, in one form or another, for centuries — which is why she treated it as a remark worth recalling rather than one worth claiming.
context.pull: Parker named her source in the same sentence. Nobody quoted that part.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Dorothy Parker, who quoted the line in a 1956 Paris Review interview and credited it to Maurice Baring. Not any single author's sentence: Quote Investigator documents the saying across 460 years, from Martin Luther's Table Talk through Poole, Steele, Swift, Pope, Guthrie and O'Malley. The text recorded here is Luther's own documented wording, the earliest form on that chain.
